introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine the reasons for the success of the League of Nations in the 1920s and its failure in the 1930s.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The League of Nations was set up by the Paris Peace Conference in 1919-20 (its Covenant formed part of the Treaty of Versailles) to maintain peace through collective security, to promote disarmament, and to encourage international cooperation. It had its headquarters at Geneva and its main organs were the Assembly, the Council, the Secretariat, the Permanent Court of International Justice and bodies such as the International Labour Organisation. In the 1920s it settled several disputes and carried out useful humanitarian work, but in the 1930s it failed to check aggression by Japan, Italy and Germany. The difference is explained by changes in the international situation, the commitment of its leading members and the weaknesses built into its structure.

**1. Reasons for the League's success in the 1920s.**
- *Settlement of minor disputes.* It resolved the dispute between Sweden and Finland over the Åland Islands in 1921 (the islands were given to Finland, with guarantees for the inhabitants), arranged the division of Upper Silesia between Germany and Poland in 1921, settled the Mosul question in 1925 (in favour of Iraq, against Turkish claims) and compelled Greece to withdraw from Bulgaria after the Petrich incident of 1925. In the Corfu dispute of 1923 Mussolini forced Greece to pay compensation, so the result was only partly successful, but the League avoided a wider conflict.
- *Support of the great powers and a favourable atmosphere.* The disputes were mostly between small states. Britain and France, the leading members, supported the League, and in the late 1920s the international climate improved: the Dawes Plan (1924), the Locarno treaties (1925), Germany's admission to the League in 1926 and the Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928), which renounced war as an instrument of national policy, encouraged faith in peaceful settlement. Economic recovery after 1924 reduced tension.
- *Humanitarian and technical work.* The League repatriated prisoners of war, helped refugees (the Nansen passport, from the work of Fridtjof Nansen), fought disease and drug trafficking, investigated slavery and forced labour, helped Austria and Hungary to recover financially, and supervised the mandates system. The International Labour Organisation improved labour standards.

**2. Reasons for failure in the 1930s.**
- *The effects of the Great Depression.* After 1929 mass unemployment and economic nationalism caused governments to concentrate on their own problems and encouraged extremist and aggressive regimes in Japan, Italy and Germany; members were reluctant to impose economic sanctions which might hurt their own trade.
- *Absence of major powers.* The United States never joined (the Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles), Germany was out until 1926 and left in 1933, Japan left in 1933 and Italy in 1937, and the Soviet Union joined only in 1934 (and was expelled in December 1939 after attacking Finland). The League lacked universal membership and military strength, and relied on Britain and France, which were themselves weakened by the economic crisis and by the memory of the First World War.
- *Structural weaknesses.* The League had no army of its own and depended on its members to enforce its decisions through economic and military sanctions; the Council required unanimity, which gave any member (including an aggressor) a veto and made action slow. The Covenant also allowed war after a delay if arbitration failed.
- *The Manchurian crisis (1931-33).* When Japan, a permanent member of the Council, invaded Manchuria after the Mukden incident of September 1931 and set up the puppet state of Manchukuo, the League sent the Lytton Commission, which condemned Japan in 1932; Japan simply left the League (1933) and no sanctions were imposed.
- *The Abyssinian crisis (1935-36).* Italy invaded Ethiopia in October 1935. The League condemned it and imposed limited sanctions that excluded oil and did not close the Suez Canal, while Britain and France sought to keep Mussolini as an ally against Hitler (the Hoare-Laval Pact of December 1935, which proposed giving Italy most of Ethiopia, was exposed and withdrawn). Ethiopia fell in 1936 and sanctions were abandoned, which destroyed the League's credibility; Emperor Haile Selassie's appeal to the League in June 1936 was ignored.
- *Disarmament and Hitler.* The Disarmament Conference (1932-34) failed, and Hitler's rearmament, the reoccupation of the Rhineland (1936), the Anschluss with Austria and the occupation of Czechoslovakia (1938-39) were done outside the League's machinery. Britain and France followed appeasement and chose to deal directly with the dictators (as at Munich in 1938) rather than through the League.

**3. Assessment.** The League succeeded when the disputing parties were small, the great powers agreed and conditions were favourable; it failed when strong states which were determined to expand defied it, the powers lacked will and common interests, and its structure did not provide means to enforce its decisions. The cause of failure was not so much the idea of collective security as the unwillingness of its leading members to apply it.

**Conclusion.** The League of Nations achieved success in the 1920s because it dealt with small disputes, had the support of Britain and France in a calm and prosperous period, and carried out valuable humanitarian work. It failed in the 1930s because the depression, the absence or withdrawal of major powers, its lack of enforcement powers and the policy of appeasement made it unable to stop Japanese, Italian and German aggression, and it was effectively replaced by the United Nations after the Second World War.
